place.en: The River Lord's shrine · The water's edge

setup.zh: 十月十八，河伯娶妇。三老坐在大伞底下，巫祝摇着铜铃；豆腐西施穿着嫁衣，坐在那只木船里。打鼓的那个，是你。
setup.en: The eighteenth of the tenth month: the River Lord's wedding. The Three Elders sit under a great umbrella, the shaman shakes her bronze bell; the Tofu Beauty sits in the wooden boat in her bridal clothes. The drummer is you.

recap.zh: 河伯祠前，你把巫祝「送去给河伯报信」；阿禾没有数数，跳下去把她捞了上来，当众报了二十五年的河伯账，巫祝自己说出了钱怎么分；三老跪着，把二十五年的河伯钱一文一文吐了出来。
recap.en: Before the shrine you "sent the shaman to take word to the River Lord"; A-He, without counting, jumped in and pulled her out, then gave twenty-five years of River Lord figures aloud, and the shaman herself told how the money was split; the Three Elders knelt and coughed up twenty-five years of River Lord money coin by coin.

zh: 打鼓的那个，脸上抹着锅底灰。
en: The eighteenth: the River Lord's wedding.
The drummer has soot on his face.

story.zh:
十月十八，河伯娶妇。那天一早，漳水边上便站满了人。三老坐在一顶大伞底下，穿着新做的绸衫，每人面前摆一盘果子。

打鼓的那个，便是沈小满。

巫祝摇着铃，绕着木船走了三圈，嘴里念念有词，然后停下来，冲着漳水高声叫道：「河伯大人——今年的新娘子，给您送来啦——」
story.en:
The eighteenth of the tenth month: the River Lord's wedding. From early morning the banks of the Zhang were packed. The Three Elders sat under a great umbrella in new silk gowns, a plate of fruit before each.

The one beating the drum was Shen Xiaoman.

The shaman shook her bell and walked three times round the boat, muttering, then stopped and cried out loud to the Zhang: "Lord of the River — this year's bride, here she comes—"

label.en: Ask the shaman to take word first

exits.means: calls the shaman's bluff: the bride is not pretty enough, so the shaman must go into the river herself and tell the River Lord

story.zh:
小满放下鼓槌，走上前去，一脸诚恳地道：「巫祝婆婆，等一下。」

他瞧了瞧船里的豆腐西施，皱起眉头，一脸为难，「这新娘子，不够好看啊。」

这一句他说得顺溜极了，一个磕巴也没打。说完，他往人堆里瞟了一眼。

小满恭恭敬敬地作了一个揖，道：「得有个人，先去河里跟河伯大人说一声：新娘子不太好看，咱们再挑挑，过几天，挑个更好看的送来。这么要紧的话，打鼓的去，不够分量。」说到这里，他抬眼看着她，「得巫祝婆婆您，亲自去。」

只听得「扑通」一声，水花溅起老高，全场鸦雀无声，几千张嘴一齐张着，合不拢。小满冲着河面拱了拱手，道：「婆婆，辛苦。」

巫祝在水里扑腾了两下，冒出头来，满头鸡毛都贴在了脸上。她张嘴喊的，却不是河伯。她喊的是：「仙长——仙长救我——」一口水灌进去，便沉了下去。岸上几千个人，只当她是在喊河伯；只有小满听得清楚，心里咯噔一下：她喊的那位「仙长」，便是那天夜里庙里那个老井嗓子。

他数到七，身后人堆里一阵乱，跟着「扑通」一声。

他转头一看，岸边泥地上扔着一件青布斗篷，斗篷上压着那本小本子，给风吹得哗哗翻页。阿禾已经不见了。她跳下去了。她没有数。人堆里有人尖着嗓子叫：「新娘子！又一个新娘子跳河了！」——方才那一闪，是一身红。

水面上冒出一个红鼻头，又沉下去，又冒出来，拖着那个一身红衣裳、一头湿鸡毛的老婆子，一点一点往岸边挪。她水性并不好，仗着筑基中成那一口长气，呛了好几口水，始终没有松手；水底下，一根青藤从她袖口里钻出去，缠住了岸边一株老柳的根，一寸一寸往回收。水浑，岸上的人瞧不见藤，只当她命大，抓着了树根。小满赶忙跳下去接应，两个人一左一右，把那老婆子拖上了岸。

巫祝吐了半天水，瘫在岸上。她睁开眼来，瞧见救她的是那夜提灯笼的阿禾，怔怔地瞧着，嘴唇哆嗦了半天，一个字也没说出来。

伞底下，胖老头先回过神来。他见巫祝活着上了岸，河面上平平的，什么也没出来，膝盖便不软了，撑着瘦老头的肩膀站起身来，指着小满，嗓门比聋老头还大：「这两个外乡人，亵渎河伯！误了吉时，明年大水，全城陪葬！还愣着做什么，推船！」

几个壮汉互相瞧了瞧，又往船边走。岸上几千个人嗡嗡的，有的往后缩，有的跟着喊「推船」。二十五年的规矩，一盏茶的工夫翻不过来。小满浑身湿透地站在船头，心里一凉：他这张嘴，到这里就用完了。

阿禾从泥地里捡起那本小本子，在湿袖子上擦了擦，翻开来。那身借来的嫁衣湿透了，贴在身上往下滴水，她嘴唇冻得发紫，声音却平平的，跟在客栈里念账一样，不高不低，一个字一个字地送出去：

「河伯钱，一户三百文，三千户，九十万文。这是我一家一家问出来的。」

胖老头的手指头还指着小满，没收回去。

「船一只，一贯。船底凿孔七个，另加二百文——刘船匠的工账上记着。嫁衣一身，八百文。香烛鼓乐，三贯。一年花五贯，余下八百九十五贯。」她翻了一页，「一年一个新娘子，二十五年，二十五只船。余下的，两万两千三百七十五贯。」

「河伯庙的瓦，漏了三年没补。这些钱，没进河里。」她抬起头来，看着伞底下那三个人，「进了伞底下这几位的口袋。」

岸上的嗡嗡声，一下子停了。

她又道：「河伯娶媳妇，娶的是活人。船底凿七个洞，是怕她活着到了河伯那里。」

瘦老头尖声道：「瞎算！一个外乡丫头，掰着指头算我们的账？谁拿了多少，你倒说说看！」

阿禾没有答他。谁拿了多少，她不知道，也不装知道。她转过身去，把那本小本子往瘫在泥里的巫祝面前一递，道：「婆婆，这八百九十五贯，是怎么分的？」

几千双眼睛，一齐落到了巫祝身上。

巫祝坐在泥里，一头湿鸡毛，看看那本子，又看看阿禾——方才在水底下死死拽着她不松手的，便是这一双手。她嘴唇抖了半天，终于道：「……是真的。」声音哑得像破锣，却一个字一个字地吐出来了，「一年结一回，娶亲那天夜里，在胖的那家后堂，当着我的面分。我一百贯；他们三家，一家二百六十五贯。」她伸出一根抖抖索索的指头，往伞底下一个一个点过去，「二十五年，他们一家六千六百二十五贯。我那一份，两千五百贯。」又道：「船底的洞，是我叫刘船匠凿的。河伯……河伯从来没跟我说过一句话。二十五年，一句也没有。」

阿禾低头在本子上添了一行，嘴唇动了一动：一百，加三个二百六十五，八百九十五。对上了。

人群后头，刘船匠蹲下去，抱住了自己的脑袋。

岸上先是静，静得听得见漳水在流。跟着，不知是谁，先往伞底下扔了一只鞋。

三老的腿，这一回是真软了。那天，三老一个也没下河。三个人跪在漳水边上，冲着河面磕头，磕得额头都青了，胖老头一面磕，一面「呜呜呜」地哭，鼻涕拖到了新绸衫上；把家里那几口箱子全抬了出来，二十五年收的河伯钱，花剩下的，一文一文全吐了出来，堆在岸上，堆成了一座小山。小满瞧见那座小山底下，压着几锭白花花的大银。

他走过去，从钱山脚下拣出一锭，翻过来，锭底朝天搁在泥地上：一个圆圈，圈里一横，连那一横往右歪的那一点，都跟开山门那天泗水码头上那一锭，歪得一模一样。

周衡也瞧见了，他没有说话。他看着那锭银子，看了很久。小满把它揣进怀里，道：「开山门那天，泗水码头上，见过一锭一样的。」周衡便没有再问。

小满回过头去。阿禾蹲在河边，拧着辫子上的水，那件斗篷又裹回了身上。他走过去，压低了声音道：「我说了，数到三十。」阿禾道：「她穿那一身湿红衣裳，顶一头鸡毛，沉下去，撑不过十个数。你那三十，是数给岸上看的。」她把辫子甩到背后，又道：「她死了，这本账就只剩外乡人一张嘴。」
story.en:
Xiaoman set down his drumsticks, stepped forward, and said with an earnest face: "Granny Shaman, wait a moment."

He looked at the Tofu Beauty in the boat, knitted his brows, and looked troubled: "This bride isn't pretty enough."

He said it smoothly, without a single stumble. When it was out, he glanced once into the crowd.

Xiaoman bowed respectfully and said: "Someone has to go into the river first and tell the River Lord: the bride's not quite pretty enough, we'll pick again and send a prettier one in a few days. A message that important — a drummer doesn't carry the weight." Here he raised his eyes to her: "It has to be you, Granny Shaman, in person."

There was a great splash, the water shot up high, and the whole bank went silent, thousands of mouths hanging open, unable to close. Xiaoman cupped his hands toward the water: "Granny, thank you for your trouble."

The shaman thrashed twice in the water and came up, her headful of chicken feathers plastered to her face. What she cried out was not the River Lord. She cried: "Immortal Master — Immortal Master, save me —" A mouthful of water went in, and she sank. The thousands on the bank took it she was calling the River Lord; only Xiaoman heard it clearly, and his heart lurched: the "Immortal Master" she called was the old-well voice in the temple that night.

At seven, there was a stir in the crowd behind him, then a splash.

He turned. A blue cloth cloak lay thrown on the mud of the bank, her little notebook weighing it down, its pages flipping in the wind. A-He was gone. She had jumped in. She had not counted. Someone in the crowd shrieked: "The bride! Another bride's jumped in!" — what had flashed past just now was red.

A red nose broke the surface, went under, came up again, towing the old woman in her red clothes and soaked chicken feathers, inching toward the bank. She was no strong swimmer; on the long breath of Foundation's Middle Attainment she swallowed mouthful after mouthful and never let go. Under the water a green vine slid out of her sleeve, wound round the roots of an old willow on the bank, and drew in, inch by inch. The water was murky; no one on the bank saw a vine — they only thought her lucky to have caught hold of a root. Xiaoman jumped in to help, and the two of them, one on each side, dragged the old woman ashore.

The shaman retched up water a long while and lay limp on the bank. She opened her eyes, saw that the one who had saved her was A-He, the girl with the lantern that night, and stared at her blankly; her lips trembled a long time, and not a word came out.

Under the umbrella, the fat old man came to himself first. Seeing the shaman ashore alive and the river lying flat, nothing coming out of it, his knees stopped being soft; he levered himself up on the thin one's shoulder and pointed at Xiaoman, louder than the deaf one: "These two outsiders blaspheme the River Lord! Miss the lucky hour, and next year the flood takes the whole city with it! What are you standing there for — push the boat!"

The strong men looked at one another and started back toward the boat. The thousands on the bank hummed; some shrank back, some took up the cry "push the boat". Twenty-five years of custom don't turn over in the time it takes to drink a cup of tea. Xiaoman stood at the bow soaked to the skin, and his heart went cold: this mouth of his had run out here.

A-He picked her little notebook up out of the mud, wiped it on her wet sleeve, and opened it. The borrowed bridal dress was soaked through, clinging and dripping, her lips blue with cold, but her voice was level, just as she read accounts at the inn, neither loud nor soft, sending out one word at a time:

"River Lord money: three hundred cash a household, three thousand households, nine hundred thousand cash. I asked it out house by house."

The fat old man's finger was still pointing at Xiaoman; he had not drawn it back.

"Boat, one: one string. Seven holes bored in the bottom: two hundred more — it's in boatwright Liu's work ledger. Bridal dress, one: eight hundred. Incense, candles, drums and pipes: three strings. Five strings spent a year; remainder, eight hundred and ninety-five strings." She turned a page. "One bride a year. Twenty-five years, twenty-five boats. The remainder: twenty-two thousand three hundred and seventy-five strings."

"The River Lord temple's roof has leaked three years and nobody's mended it. This money didn't go into the river." She raised her head and looked at the three under the umbrella. "It went into the pockets of the gentlemen under that umbrella."

The humming on the bank stopped all at once.

She went on: "When the River Lord takes a wife, he takes a living girl. You bore seven holes in the boat because you're afraid she'll reach him alive."

The thin old man shrieked: "Made up! An outsider girl doing our sums on her fingers? Who took how much — go on, tell us!"

A-He didn't answer him. Who took how much she didn't know, and she didn't pretend to. She turned and held the notebook out to the shaman lying in the mud: "Granny — these eight hundred and ninety-five strings. How were they split?"

Thousands of eyes fell on the shaman at once.

The shaman sat in the mud, a headful of wet feathers, and looked at the notebook, then at A-He — these were the hands that had gripped her under the water and never let go. Her lips trembled a long while; at last she said: "…It's true." Her voice was hoarse as a cracked gong, but she got it out word by word. "Settled once a year, on the night of the wedding, in the fat one's back hall, split in front of me. A hundred strings to me; their three houses, two hundred and sixty-five each." She put out one shaking finger and pointed under the umbrella, one by one. "Twenty-five years: six thousand six hundred and twenty-five strings a house. My share, two thousand five hundred." And: "I had boatwright Liu bore the holes. The River Lord… the River Lord never said one word to me. Twenty-five years, not one."

A-He bent her head and added a line to her notebook, her lips moving a little: one hundred, plus three times two hundred and sixty-five, eight hundred and ninety-five. It tallied.

At the back of the crowd, Liu the boatwright squatted down and held his head in his hands.

First the bank went silent, so silent you could hear the Zhang flowing. Then someone — no one knew who — threw a shoe under the umbrella first.

This time the Three Elders' legs truly gave way. That day not one of the Three Elders went into the river. The three of them knelt by the Zhang knocking their heads toward the water until their foreheads were bruised — the fat one bawling "Waaah, waaah" as he knocked, snot trailing onto his new silk gown — had every chest in their houses carried out, and coughed up, coin by coin, what was left of twenty-five years of River Lord money, heaped on the bank into a little mountain. Xiaoman saw, at the foot of that little mountain, a few big ingots of white silver.

He went over, picked an ingot from the foot of the money-heap, turned it over and set it base-up in the mud: a circle, with one stroke across it — down to the little slant of the stroke to the right, slanted exactly like the ingot on the Si River shore the day the gate opened.

Zhou Heng saw it too, and said nothing. He looked at the ingot for a long time. Xiaoman put it inside his jacket and said: "The day the gate opened, on the Si River shore — I saw one just like it." Zhou Heng asked nothing more.

Xiaoman looked round. A-He was crouched at the water's edge wringing out her braids, the cloak wrapped round her again. He went over and said low: "I said I'd count to thirty." A-He said: "In that soaked red dress with a headful of feathers, she'd go under and not last ten. Your thirty was counted for the bank." She flicked her braids behind her and added: "If she dies, this book is only an outsider's word."

exits.means: runs away, leaves the girl, refuses to act

text.zh: 你走出两步，又停下。船里的姑娘在看你。
text.en: You take two steps, and stop. The girl in the boat is looking at you.
